analysis.explanation: The Random Forest classifies this binary as malware with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking, with a combined SHAP contribution of about +0.17. Two groups of n-grams are consistent with the compute profile of a mining workload. The first is a rotate/add (ARX-style) cluster: MOV ROL (+0.010115), ROL ADD (+0.008449), ADD ROL (+0.007946), ADD ROR (+0.007202) and ROL MOV (+0.006078). Rotate-and-add chains are typical of hash and cipher round functions. The second is a SIMD state-manipulation cluster: PXOR MOVAPS (+0.024413, the strongest feature), PXOR MOVUPS (+0.013940), MOVUPS PXOR (+0.006139) and PADDQ MOVDQA (+0.005637). These match vectorized XOR and add operations on wide blocks of data, as in hashing or cipher inner loops. Floating-point conversion and multiply patterns (ADD CVTSI2SD, CVTSI2SD MULSD) and bit-scan patterns (DEC BSR, BSF MOV) add weaker support. Several n-grams are generic and occur in ordinary compiled code: CALL RET, PUSH RET, TEST JGE, LEA POP, SUB CMOVG, and PCMPEQB PMOVMSKB, which is a common vectorized byte-scan idiom. Their contribution here is mainly statistical. All n-gram frequencies are very low (at most 0.000404), and the evidence lists no function-level locations, so the assessment rests on the combined pattern and the model's output, not on a confirmed mining routine. Overall the evidence supports a high-confidence cryptojacking classification, with the caveat that it is indirect and should be confirmed by reverse engineering.

evidence_analysis.assessment: The top feature. A vector XOR followed by an aligned 128-bit move is consistent with SIMD state mixing or buffer initialization in hash or cipher loops. It is the largest single driver toward the cryptojacking label.
A vector XOR followed by an unaligned 128-bit store or load. It supports SIMD block-processing code of the kind used in mining or crypto primitives, and it reinforces the PXOR/MOV* pattern.
A generic control-flow pattern, probably a thin wrapper or tail stub. It has little intrinsic meaning but contributes statistically in this model.
A load or move followed by a bitwise rotation, which is typical of hash round functions (ARX-style constructions). Part of the rotate cluster.
Branchless compare-and-select arithmetic. It is common in optimized numeric code and is weakly suggestive of tight compute loops.
A generic sign-test branch. It is relatively frequent (0.000404) and not specific to mining, so it is a weak, non-specific contributor.
Rotate followed by add is the core ARX pattern in hash and stream-cipher rounds. Combined with ADD ROL, it supports a hashing-like compute kernel.
The reverse ordering of the ARX pair. At frequency 0.000127 it is among the more frequent rotate-related features, which supports repeated round-function-like operations.
A vectorized byte-comparison and mask-extraction idiom. It is common in optimized string and memory scanning routines and is not inherently mining-specific, but it indicates SIMD-heavy code.
Add followed by rotate-right. It is another ARX-style variant consistent with cryptographic hash round operations.
Integer arithmetic followed by integer-to-double conversion. It indicates mixed integer and floating-point computation, possibly for hashrate or statistics calculation, but this is not conclusive.
An unusual control-flow sequence at very low frequency (0.000001). It may reflect tiny stubs or obfuscated or optimized code, with limited interpretability.
An integer-to-double conversion followed by a floating-point multiply. It suggests scaling or numeric computation and adds mild support alongside the integer/SIMD patterns.
An unaligned vector load followed by XOR. At frequency 0.000222 it is relatively common and fits SIMD XOR-based mixing of data blocks.
A rotate followed by a move of the result. It is part of the rotation-heavy cluster consistent with hash round computations.
A decrement followed by a bit-scan-reverse. It is used in bit-length and normalization computations, including big-number arithmetic. It is a weak, ambiguous contributor.
A bit-scan-forward followed by a move. It is commonly used in optimized bit manipulation and is weakly consistent with low-level numeric or hashing code.
A packed 64-bit add followed by an aligned vector move. It matches vectorized 64-bit lane arithmetic used in hash and cipher inner loops.
A generic address computation followed by a stack pop, typical of function epilogues. It has little specific meaning and contributes mainly statistically.
Integer add followed by a 64-bit SIMD/GPR move. It is consistent with moving 64-bit state between scalar and vector registers in vectorized hashing code, though it is not conclusive.

key_indicators: The model output is MALWARE at probability 1.0000, and all 20 top SHAP features push toward cryptojacking
A rotate/add (ARX-style) cluster: MOV ROL, ROL ADD, ADD ROL, ADD ROR, ROL MOV
A SIMD XOR/add cluster: PXOR MOVAPS (+0.024413, the top feature), PXOR MOVUPS, MOVUPS PXOR, PADDQ MOVDQA
Supporting numeric patterns: ADD CVTSI2SD, CVTSI2SD MULSD, DEC BSR, BSF MOV
Generic control-flow n-grams (CALL RET, TEST JGE, LEA POP, PUSH RET) contribute statistically but are not specific to mining
No function-level locations are provided and all n-gram frequencies are very low, which limits certainty
analysis.recommended_action: Treat the sample as likely cryptojacking malware and analyze it in an isolated sandbox. Locate the functions containing the rotate/add and PXOR/PADDQ sequences and check whether they implement a hash or cipher round loop. Disassemble them to confirm a mining kernel, and look for constants identifying the algorithm. Also check for network configuration, such as pool connections, and for persistence. Block and quarantine the sample pending confirmation.
